speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this week, April 18 to 24, is National Volunteer Week.
This is an opportunity for all of us to express our heartfelt thanks to the more than 13 million Canadians who volunteer their time, skills and energies to enhance the quality of life in their community.
We cannot repeat often enough how much we appreciate their commitment and the services they provide. Volunteers have become an essential and vital part of Canadian society and a major economic resource.
Through their work, volunteers have made a major contribution to this country. We have everything to gain as a society by maintaining this tradition of generosity and caring.
I suggest we take this opportunity to urge people to join those 13 million volunteers across the country. Since this is their week, I think it is appropriate to say how proud we are of what they do, and I want to say: thank you.

Mr. Speaker, the former Minister of Justice, the current
defence minister, promised additional amendments to the Young Offenders Act. We never saw them. The new minister suggests that some young offenders be publicly identified. However in a letter to a victim's family he says just the opposite, that publication of the young offender's identity may foster an illusion of public safety.
Canadians are tired of empty promises and illusions. They demand substance. The village of Belcarra in my riding of Port Moody-Coquitlam wants a full review of the youth justice system, a national and public gathering of those who have something to say about youth crime and a frank discussion of what is wrong with the act. So far 124 B.C. municipalities agree.
I support this effort. We need to know the full extent of youth crime and what is happening with present youth court sentencing, post-custody supervision and rehabilitative programs before we can make improvements to the act.
I hope the Minister of Justice is listening to the village of Belcarra and the other voices in Canada that are calling for a review of youth crime and our response to it.

Mr. Speaker, there are now over four million Canadians living under Statistics Canada's low-income cut-off line.
A woman from my riding is one of those Canadians forgotten and ignored by the current administration. The woman in question was disabled in a car accident two years ago. Since that time she and her son have had to face the horrific reality faced by 47,000 Manitobans, the horrific reality of poverty.
This includes having to make do on less than $20,000 annually for a family of two; being forced, in her case, to cover the cost of medication not covered under Pharma-care, in excess of $1,000 a year; and facing financial

April 21, 1993
barriers to post-secondary education, where she could do more for herself and her son. That is not to mention the emotional problems and stress involved in trying to get by with so little.

On top of that, Tories in Manitoba are blindly imitating their federal counterparts and making irresponsible cuts in programs targeted to the neediest in our society.
It is time Canada and this government showed they are prepared to fight poverty and the very serious problems it generates.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, April 22, is Earth Day. Earth Day reminds us of the precious living treasures we share in our common home, Earth, and that although we have a right to use these gifts there is an equal responsibility to preserve and improve the earth and the quality of life it supports.
Earth Day 1993 is dedicated to a tree planting theme. It is a fitting theme, as the planting of trees is symbolic of environmental awareness and commitment.
In the words of the dedicated individuals of the Earth Day Canada Organization:
The image of putting down roots and contributing to the future
gives us a feeling of well-being and a connection with nature.
In addition, the tree planting theme is a good complement to the government's Tree Plant Canada program initiated under the green plan. The $75 million, six-year initiative is designed to foster and encourage the planting of up to 325 million trees in Canada.
Those involved in making this year's Earth Day theme a reality deserve our thanks and the thanks of generations yet to come.

Mr. Speaker, in the very near future the Minister of Finance is expected to present a new budget in the House.
What do Canadians have to show for nine years of Conservative economic management? Thanks to unending tax increases the average middle class family now spends almost $2,000 more per year than it did in 1984. That family now spends 44 per cent of its income on taxes and real after-tax income has declined.
Conservative economic management also gave us the worst recession since the Great Depression. We now have over 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, 2.2 million on welfare and 2 million relying on food banks.
We have lost 325,000 manufacturing jobs since 1989 and over 200,000 people and small businesses have gone bankrupt.
It is clear it is time for change.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw attention to a case of great concern to thousands of Canadians and more specifically to people in the Fraser Valley.
Two young Canadians, Christine Lamont and David Spencer, have been serving time in a Brazilian jail since 1989. These two people were arrested for their involvement in the kidnapping of a wealthy Brazilian businessman. They denied knowledge of the kidnapping but were convicted and sentenced.
I know the government, specifically the minister of external affairs, has maintained a strong interest in this case and made efforts through diplomatic channels on behalf of these two Canadians. As well, a treaty between Brazil and Canada to facilitate prisoner transfers is completed and awaits ratification and implementation.
There have been reports of terrible conditions in Brazilian jails. As well, there are indications that sanitary conditions in some jails are below adequate standards. I
April 21, 1993

realize that information from the media does not give the full picture but it does raise concerns.
Considering the conditions that Lamont and Spencer find themselves in and the unfinished nature of the prisoner transfer agreement I ask if there is any further assistance the minister and her officials can give these people.

Mr. Speaker, Mexico's lack of financial resources makes it necessary for the government to ensure that NAFTA, if implemented, works to improve the environment through environmental standards that would be enforced in Mexico as well as at home and in the U.S.A.
One approach would be to impose trade sanctions. A better approach would be to launch funding initiatives such as creating a North American development bank. It would provide Mexico with funds to construct sewers, sewage treatment plants and water purification systems as well as finance programs to reduce pesticide use, increase energy efficiency, improve public transportation and reduce pollution.
The bank could trigger private sector financing with the result of substantial benefits in the form of improved human health and quality of life, a clean environment and a healthy economy.
Will the government adopt this approach or accept the indifference shown so far by the Minister for International Trade?

Mr. Speaker, the National Transportation Agency is now holding public hearings on the acquisition of 34 per cent of Canadian
International shares by American Airlines, the U.S. giant.
By approving this transaction, the government would sign the death warrant of the Gemini reservation system, and any chances of having a genuine Canadian transportation network would be doomed.
In its push to promote competition at any cost, the Tory government is about to turn our Canadian carriers into mere northern arms of major U.S. carriers.
Last summer the Minister of Transport openly sided with PWA against Air Canada, with Calgary against Montreal, by spending enormous sums to subsidize Canadian. He has opted for competition regardless of the cost, to the detriment of the civil aviation industry in this country.
If he really wants to let the market decide, the minister should stop giving in to pressure from the west and allow the creation of a genuine Canadian monopoly with international stature. Most major countries in the world have this kind of system, something they can be proud of.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here is something to crow about.
I quote from an article in The Globe and Mail entitled "Confidence in Mr. Crow". It says:
Mr. Crow has scored an impressive hat trick: low inflation, low interest rates, and a lower exchange rate. He has achieved all three, however, because he had just one goal in mind: low inflation. It is useful to think what would have happened had he not been so single-minded. As inflation rose, Canada's creditors would have sold our bonds, and gone on selling until interest rates rose enough to compensate them. Foreigners dumping their Canadian dollar holdings would have set off a cascading decline in the exchange rate, far overshooting its long-run value. With the prices of domestic and imported goods rising, workers would have demanded higher wage increases, and we'd be off on another inflationary spiral. Without confidence, all is lost.
That is the Crow rate. To the opposition I say: "Let them eat crow."

Oral Questions
April 21, 1993

Mr. Speaker, since the Conservatives took office Canadian manufacturing productivity has grown at only two-thirds the rate of the G-7.
I invite all people, all members of this House, to promote volunteerism within their communities and to recommend worthy individuals for next year's awards.
Over the past four years Canada has lost 365,000, or 18 per cent, of its manufacturing jobs. To help reverse this decline and increase our competitiveness the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is proposing to introduce ISO-9000 quality standards, already adopted in Europe and Japan, to Canada.
The CMA has even offered to run this program for the government and can do so for less money than this government spent on its still-born prosperity agenda.
Now that the government has the opportunity to do something really practical, it refuses. Other governments work co-operatively with their manufacturers but not ours. It is little wonder we are mired in 11 per cent unemployment. We urge the industry minister to reconsider his refusal to co-operate with our Canadian manufacturers and introduce this ISO-9000 program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week is National Volunteer Week.
I would like to remind members of this unique national program sponsored by the Department of National Health and Welfare. This program recognizes the enormous contributions of volunteers to their communities and to their country as a whole.
Since 1977 hundreds of caring and committed Canadian volunteers have been recognized through the Canada volunteer award program. Each year the department presents Canada volunteer award medals and certificates to those Canadians who have made outstanding voluntary contributions toward improving the health and social well-being of their fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has been told by the Chamber of Commerce to cut social programs, unemployment insurance, and federal support to Canadians and their families. This approach of forcing the burden of paying off the huge debt that the Liberals and Conservatives have created onto the least affluent in Canada has been a disaster.
Statistics Canada tells us that 94 per cent of our debt is a result of high interest rates and tax breaks to the rich and profitable corporations and only 6 per cent is a result of government program spending, all spending not just social spending. Yet this government insists on trying to solve the problem by attacking social programs.
The contrast to deficit control measures of provincial governments is striking. The New Democrat approach in Saskatchewan has the support of a substantial proportion of the population and has been one of compassion so as to spare the least affluent as much as possible.
There is a better approach. Before the Minister of Finance finalizes his budget I hope he will contact the minister of finance of the New Democratic Government of Saskatchewan to get her advice on how to actually reduce the deficit and do so without attacking the most vulnerable in our society.

According to the British press there was only one director who stood against the wishes of the bank's president, Mr. Attali, and it was Mr. McCutchan, the Canadian representative. We have learned that he has been called back to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, there are two completely wrong statements in what the Leader of the Opposition said.
He said that I found what Mr. Attali did completely unacceptable and he also said that the Minister of Finance referred to Jacques Attali as incompetent. That is completely false. The two statements are wrong.
I clearly explained that we supported Mr. Attali as chief executive in pursuing important policies of the bank for Europe and Russia, but that we had instructed our agent to vote against a budget where there were administrative abuses. The two are perfectly reconcilable and there is nothing wrong there. Let us stop dealing in gossip and talking nonsense like the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, let us try to understand from the minister's reply the situation as it is today.
Back in January we had an expression of concern from the Minister of Finance to the President of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development about the way in which the bank was being administered.
Then the Canadian director was instructed by the government not only to express further concern about the administration of the bank but to vote against the 1993 budget. The Canadian director was the only director who did so.
Then the Prime Minister, according to the London press and the president himself, called the president and said he had the "continued support" of the Canadian government. The Prime Minister today says the Canadian support relates only to the activities of the bank in eastern Europe. It does not relate to the administration of the bank. We voted against his administration we criticized the bank's administration. Which is it?
Are we dividing our support for the bank? Are we saying on the one hand that the administration is no good at all, we agree with the British and others on that but on the other hand it is doing all right in eastern Europe?
Would the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance please tell the House what the Canadian policy is vis-a-vis the bank.

In that regard, in January I sent a letter to all of my G-7 colleagues expressing concern about the expenditures by all international financial institutions, including the World Bank, the IMF and the EBRD. As a matter of fact in part I said: "We are all attempting to minimize public service costs and constrain wage expectations and in comparison recent increases in IFIs, international financial institutions, administrative costs appear to be definitely out of line". I went on to say: "In my view IFIs should not be exempt from the realities facing the private sector and the governments of each of our countries."
What was happening was that our director was following through on government policy and voted against what he considered to be an excessive budget, as we have voted against excessive pay increases in other financial institutions as well, and so the policy is consistent right across the board.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The finance minister claimed last week that the dominant issue facing Canadians was the deficit and that the way to tackle this deficit was to continue the failed Tory economic policies that we have had over the last nine years. I might add that the same failed policies have more than doubled the debt since this government came into power and have resulted in this government being $10 billion over its target for deficit reduction had been.
It is clear that the government's economic policies have failed Canadians, have failed to reduce the deficit and have failed to reduce the debt. Will the minister consider changing course, making the choices that will

April 21, 1993

address both the fiscal deficit and the tragedy created by increasing unemployment in this country?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians believe and hopefully some day the leader of the NDP will believe in the concept that deficit reduction and control of the debt are key to growth in the economy, key to the creation of jobs and key to confidence in the economy. Even her friend, the premier of the province of Ontario, is starting to realize that.
Clearly the premier of Saskatchewan realized that fact when he brought in a very tough and difficult budget. That budget can clearly be termed as nothing other than being a tight-fisted budget, a budget that is touting austerity as the headline in The Financial Post alluded to this morning.
I know that there is a fundamental difference in economic philosophy as it applies to the government and the New Democratic Party, but I think we are on the side of Canadians when they have clearly registered in massive numbers their concern over the deficit. We hope to address that in the budget when I bring it down.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
There is no question of the concern that everyone feels about the deficit and the debt. There is a real debate about how we address that and whether we address it by creating unemployment and more unemployment as this government has done or whether we address it by reducing unemployment so we can create more taxpayers to truly address the debt and the deficit.
This government's policies have cost Canada over 400,000 manufacturing jobs. Not only do we see the loss of jobs, but we also see the loss to communities and individuals. Today we have representatives from 2,500 workers who will lose their jobs if GM closes its foundry plant in St. Catharines. This is the human face, the real face of unemployment, the real result.
If the minister wants to convince somebody about changing opinions he should talk to the one in four Canadians who are looking for jobs because they know that is the real problem.
Since the Minister of Finance is going to be bringing in a last budget before the election, will he really begin to address those 2,500 workers from St. Catharines and the 1.5 million other unemployed and those 2 million underemployed and provide some hope and work for Canadians so we can truly address the debt and the deficit?

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, I am raising a question of privilege with respect to yesterday's vote. I will now continue my remarks.
Yesterday at 3 p.m. the Acting Speaker called in the members to put the question on Bill C-62. After the bells rang for 15 minutes, the Acting Speaker read the motion and asked all members who were in favour of the motion to rise. After all Conservative members had voted, the Acting Speaker rose and asked all those opposed to please rise. The Liberal leader rose, with all Liberal members present, as did the members of the New Democratic Party, and we in the Bloc Quebecois did the same.
Subsequently, the Acting Speaker rose and again asked those opposed to please rise. We in the Bloc Quebecois immediately voiced our disapproval of this procedure, which created considerable confusion in the House and led me to rise on a point of order. My point of order was not allowed until after the Clerk had read the results of the vote, which was 223 yeas and no nays.
My point of order was duly reported in Hansard of April 20, at page 18183. In my point of order, I mentioned to the Acting Speaker that we had voted against the motion. However, the Chair did not bother to reply
or even comment but instead proceeded with the question on the main motion.
I have a video of what happened yesterday during the vote. If you wish, I can leave this copy with you as evidence.
My colleagues and I were quick to express our disagreement even before the results of the division were read. Beauchesne's fifth edition, citation 223(5), page 76, has this to say:
An error noted during a division may be corrected before the total
is announced.
As I said before, I raised a point of order immediately, as indicated in the same edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, page 78, citation 235.
Consequently, I ask that division No. 458 be recorded in Hansard to reflect how the members of the Bloc voted, which was "nay", and that Hansard of April 20, 1993 be corrected accordingly. I ask this only on behalf of the members of the Bloc Quebecois, since the Liberals and the New Democrats did not ask me to speak on their behalf.
However, Mr. Speaker, if you think that my question of privilege is a reflection on a vote of the House in the meaning of Standing Order 18,1 would ask that Division No. 458 be rescinded.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to bring before the House a bill to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Immigration Act, and the Narcotic Control Act, as well as the Psychoactive Substance Control Act.
I have two brief quotes I would like to put on the record before providing a quick understanding of the three clauses. In 1923 in this Chamber without a single member speaking, marijuana was criminalized and in fact since then we have seen the penalties increase to the point that some marijuana offences now cany life imprisonment as the sanction in this country. It is the strongest sanction outside Malaysia and Thailand where people are executed.
Emily Murphy, a judge in Alberta in 1922, wrote in the book The Black Candle the following, which I think explains why many Canadians took an unusual view toward marijuana for a long time:
Persons using this narcotic smoke the dried leaves of the plant, which has the effect of driving them completely insane. The addict loses all sense of moral responsibility. Addicts to this drug, while under its influence, are immune to pain and could be severely injured without having any realization of their condition.
While in this condition they become raving maniacs and are liable to kill or indulge in any form of violence to other persons using the most savage methods of cruelty without, as said before, any sense of moral responsibility. When coming under the influence of this narcotic these victims present the most horrible condition imaginable. They are dispossessed of their natural and normal willpower and their mentality is that of idiots. If this drug is indulged in to any great extent, it ends in the untimely death of the addict.
.(1515)

In debating this issue I would like to bring to the attention of my colleagues two or three amendments that my colleague from St. Boniface has introduced to improve the bill. It would otherwise not be supportable because it is unfair to our social scientists and to our scientists involved in the humanities.
The amendments will ensure that there is security of funding for the social sciences and humanities and will secure the identity, integrity and importance of these disciplines. If this bill is passed as improved with these amendments there will be accountability to Parliament.
Motion No. 32 proposes that the separate mandate of the new agency, which will include research, arts and international cultural relations, be funded through separate budget appropriation votes in the House of Commons.
The importance of this approach is to ensure that not all of them are taken right away. We must not forget one very important segment of the total, and that is the social sciences and humanities review. We would like to ensure that funding for this discipline is continued and have shown the value of this discipline.
Having practised medicine for some time before entering politics, I know the importance of the social and humanities discipline even in the practise of medicine. We need our social scientists if we are going to take care of the whole patient. Their importance can be multiplied many times in other disciplines as well.
On the second point, the security of identity of this discipline, Motion No. 24 would reflect, if accepted, a change of name from Canada Council for the arts, research, social sciences and humanities, to the arts, social sciences and humanities Research Council of Canada. In essence, this proposal would truly reflect a merger of the two and not the abolition of one and the retention of the other.
You got that right.

It is human nature that in order to give importance and recognition to any group, its identity has to be retained and recognized. Recognition of its identity and integrity is an important tool in ensuring and enhancing its continued productivity. I do not think this government is prepared to tell the House of Commons and Canadians that this discipline is no longer important. If it is not it ought to be reasonable and accept this very reasonable proposal.
The government has argued that the rationale for merging the two agencies is to develop efficiency and effectiveness. Critical in any measurement of efficiency and effectiveness is the important need to have a tool to monitor the program and ensure accountability. Motion No. 40, as proposed by my colleague from St. Boniface would reflect this need for accountability and monitoring of whatever new changes are made. We would like a parliamentary review committee to review the function of the new entity and agency five years after the legislation comes into effect. It is a reasonable proposal that this government can truly ill afford not to adopt.
There are many more issues that I would like to address. In the interest of maintaining the importance of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council as well as the Canada Council, I think our proposals are very reasonable. The proposed amendments strike at the heart of the concerns that these groups have brought to the attention of this government.
On December 2, 1992 the Canadian Association of University Teachers made a very useful observation when it indicated, and I quote: "Its profound disappointment with the government's decision to merge the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council with the Canada Council without any consultation with the stakeholders involved." Lately we have been hearing from the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to clarify a number of issues but I want to begin by saying that what we are doing here is simply combining two organizations to save administration costs. Today people are concerned about tax dollars and where they are being spent. I think they would applaud this kind of streamlining move which really just reduces some of the overburden and additional cost of carrying two administrations. Let me break this down a little bit.
First of all, there was reference made in an article to a figure of $1.5 million suggesting that that would be the net savings for five years. That is not correct. The savings will actually be $5 million per year.
I think that is a worthwhile number of dollars to attempt to save through the combining of two administrations. The savings that will accrue to us because we have taken that step. That $5 million will kick in probably starting in the third-year operation of the council.
One will notice in other streamlining procedures in the private sector that it is usually two or three years down the road before one begins to see the net savings. There is an upfront cost associated with this. However, we think $5 million a year is worth the effort. We know that this is what the figures will be because we have had advice, contrary to what my hon. friend opposite said, from the boards themselves. We talked to the Canada Council, SSHRC and the Treasury Board.
Let me just give an example of how these savings are realized. For example, we will have a streamlined program structure. We will have much simpler, more flexible financial management to deal with. We will only be dealing with one location. Instead of paying two rents we will be paying one. We will have rationalized common services. For example, we will only have one personnel manager, we will only have one financial manager and we will only have one council instead of two.
All of this makes sense for a savings of $5 million a year, at a time when we have to find more innovative and efficient ways to deal with our tax dollars and the expenditures that are putting such pressure on our debt and the deficit that we have to contend with.
I think it is important also to remember that these two councils operated as one for over 20 years, so this is not new. It is not a tremendously unusual departure from what was normal. For 20 years they worked as one council. That is an important point.
We will remember that the council developed a structure that had adapted to two clienteles. It had no trouble with the creation of an academic advisory panel as a parallel to the advisory arts panel, and the establishment of a separate administrative staff to deal with the academic community.
At that time the differentiation of the roles between the two was fully understood and accepted by the two bodies and their relationship was characterized by mutual respect. I say this to my hon. friend across the way.
I think we should also note that in its appointment of the new council the government of the day, which was the Liberal administration, took the Canada Council as its model and gave the new body, SSHRC, the same kind of composition in terms of its board and similar budgetary and expenditure practices.
These two organizations are very similar and they have a long history that goes back to a time when they were actually one. We are not creating any hardship here for anybody in the community. As a matter of fact, the government is committed to keeping the three budgets separate for each of the council's clients so there will not be any confusion about who gets what or whether or not the humanities people will get their fair share of the funding or the grants. That will not be a problem because they will be kept separate.
April 21, 1993

The Treasury Board has already met with the management of the two existing councils to see how this can be achieved administratively and to iron out the technical details.
Also, Bill C-93 says:
The government shall have regard to the importance of maintaining
a broadly representative membership that reflects the function of the
Council.
What this means in practical terms is that the council will represent the interests not only of the artistic and academic communities, but of all Canadians. That is what we want. We want the agencies that we fund in Ottawa to reflect the broad interests of all Canadians. If we can save money at the same time I think we are accomplishing what most Canadians would like us to accomplish.
I might also mention that some points were made yesterday that perhaps require some clarification. There was a discussion, for example, of the calculation of the percentage of administration overhead. As a matter of fact, it was the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle on page 18158 of Hansard who used some percentages that I think were intended as an expression of the administrative costs in relation to total costs.
In other words, the dollars that we spend on grants and the numbers of dollars that have been distributed will rise as they have done over the years. However, the administrative costs are fairly standard. One cannot make comparisons of the administrative costs today with the administrative costs of yesterday because obviously the costs today would be lower because the grants are higher. The costs are still significant. As we see, $5 million can be saved by streamlining the administration of the two.
Another comment was made about 200 per cent CPI inflation. When the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance mentioned this, the hon. member for Terrebonne, he referred to the 200 per cent increase in the administrative costs. What he was talking about was nominal dollars. He did not in his speech discount for inflation in that period.
What we are saying is that as a point of comparison, the growth in the administrative costs since 1977-78 have actually exceeded the rate of CPI inflation. That is where we are going to realize those savings by reducing the
Government Orders
administration and streamlining and actually saving a total of $5 million a year which is not, as one will agree, an insignificant amount of money. It certainly underlines the necessity of combining these two agencies so that Canadian taxpayers could realize the benefit of a far more efficient and streamlined operation.
The Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada people will be looked after. Their interests will be protected. They will continue to receive grants and be able to continue the work that they do which is so important to the country. However, we will be saving money overall because we are taking a more practical and efficient approach to the way we deal with these agencies.
I also want to point something out about voting. We are not saying that there will be one vote for appropriation purposes. The ministers and Treasury Board will decide how many votes there will be. They will doubtless take into account the wishes of the management and the views of the two boards. There will be input from the people who are most impacted and most affected in spite of what my hon. colleague for Winnipeg North said a few moments ago.
Finally, I want to point out that $35 million will be the combined administrative overhead for all three of the agencies. It is included in the $217 million which is a total of all the funding, including the overhead, the grants and so on for all three sectors.
Again, just to underline what I have said before, when we combine these agencies there will be a net savings of $5 million a year starting in the third year. Those are significant dollars. If we take a look at it over a 10-year period, it will be more than $5 million because obviously inflation on an annual basis will have taken those administrative costs well beyond that.
I hope I have clarified things. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on this today.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg South did not clarify neither for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North or for the members of this House of Commons. This is because she talks about $5 million in savings that would be accrued by merging the two organizations that we are debating today, yet we really do not know where she pulled those $5 million statistics from.

My colleague for St. Boniface who has been doing a yeoman's job for our side on this particular committee has said in the debate, both in committee and in the Chamber, that no such reports, findings or studies have ever been produced by government members or by civil servants who have come forward before the committee.
One would think, if there was any truth to the suggestion that there would be savings of $5 million plus, then at some point during the committee stage some bureaucrat, minister or government member would have put that testimony before the appropriate committee or in fact documented that particular study. To date, no official has ever shown any study proving that there will be savings.
We know and we have heard from various officials themselves that there will be a $1 million start-up cost. I do not think it should be simply a given and automatic for one to say that collapsing two different houses that provide roofs over these organizations into one bigger house with one bigger bureaucracy will save dollars.
No one has a monopoly on trying to be fiscally responsible in this Chamber. In the end we all represent that same taxpayer with the dollars. One of our functions is to spend those moneys wisely and frugally.
It is not good enough to have this member of Parliament or this government thinking, without any evidence and with simple assumptions, that it will save all sorts of dollars by collapsing two homes into one.
Second, there has not been one study or report that shows that the one new organization would either be more efficient or effective. Once again, in committee, when challenged, no officials were able to point to any type of evidence that would suggest that on an effectiveness and efficiency factor the new organization would be superior to what is being produced now.
Third, some government members and officials only a while back were actually considering withdrawing their proposal for an amalgamation of the Canada Council
with the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council because they knew that they had not proven their case. Notwithstanding that, they continued.
We heard the story before that government members have come to us to try to approve some types of different organizational structures or promises on the grounds that it would save Canadian taxpayers all sorts of dollars. That case has yet to be proven in a very tangible and substantive way.
The other factor that I think is a particularly hurtful one in this equation is that there has been little or no consultation with the affected personnel in either division. That speaks to the type of governance that we have had for nine years. Perhaps that is the type of talk used by one of the ministers in the leadership race when speaking about the new style of politics. This comes because people are tired of the Conservative brand of politics in terms of the politics of inclusion. Here is a perfect case in point where scientists, researchers and academics were not even consulted with respect to the possible merger of these two organizations.
In fact, I received a copy of a letter from the Association of University Teachers. It was addressed to the right hon. Prime Minister and in its opening paragraph it says:
I am writing this open letter to you to express our profound
disappointment with your government's decision to merge the Social
Sciences and Humanities Research Council with the Canada Council
without any consultation with the stakeholders involved.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a a point of order. I apologize for interrupting the hon. member but before five o'clock I have to indicate that tomorrow will be an allotted day.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention that we have in this country over 100 universities, 13,000 to
15,000	social scientists, over 200,000 people represented by the arts community and close to 30,000 Canadian academics. That is a fairly impressive and significant constituency.
When one talks about two councils that directly impact on this significant constituency one would think that it would be normal, prudent and logical for the government to consult the stakeholders of that constituency.
April 21, 1993

However, when those individuals come before the committee and write to the Prime Minister of the country to say that they have not even been consulted, what kind of decision making do we really have?
If we are truly concerned with the output and substance of the work those two councils do and if we are serious about the work they produce on behalf of Canadians then clearly and surely one would think that a government before moving to combine the two organizations would not only make a convincing argument based on fact, and not based on perception, but would also consult the various stakeholders. That is without even talking about the best interests of Canadians at the end of the day.
From these vantage points my friend from St. Boniface and others who have been engaged very seriously and in detail on this bill have moved a series of amendments that would speak to that accountability, that would speak to providing the facts rather than perceptions and myths.
I do not think it was too much to ask in those amendments for a greater accountability by the government rather than dropping figures loosely on the floor of the House of Commons and then going somewhere else to speak to the actual facts in the matter.
We have been somewhat disillusioned because the significant constituency I quoted moments ago has not even been consulted; because no official, minister or government member has had the foresight to document their arguments on effectiveness and cost savings, and because we are actually trying to make it more accountable with Motion No. 40, put forward by my colleague from St. Boniface, which tries to make it more accountable than the government is suggesting as we wish to have an accountability review every five years rather than the longer term suggested by this government.
We do not need to be lectured or preached to in terms of who is more accountable. We all have to be fiscally responsible but we do not accept as a given arguments that are based and founded on political quicksand rather than on hard scientific facts.

Therefore, having been refused at the committee stage we are appealing through the Chair to the government during this important report stage of Bill C-93 to listen once again to those arguments, not for our sake but for the sake of the important constituency that is out there working on behalf of Canadians and our country and enriching that vibrant life which is part of this Canadian mosaic.
On behalf of members of a very important constituency who surely cannot all be wrong, at least give those people the time of day to listen to their arguments. After all, as I quoted from the letter, they are the real stakeholders in this case. speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. For your information and that of the House, in his speech the hon. member challenged the facts presented by my colleague from Winnipeg and myself concerning potential savings of $5 million. I would now like to conclude, if I may, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I cannot accept this point of order because it is really a matter of opinion and opinions can differ. The rules of debate are very strict and this is not a point of order per se.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to say a few words regarding report stage of Bill C-93. I want to make my comment in the context that we all acknowledge the fact that we are in a knowledge-based economy in which education, training and research is critical and paramount in terms of future positive economic growth in Canada and full employment for Canadians. That is why most of us are shocked, and that is putting it mildly, to see that the government is determined to proceed with part III of Bill C-93.

April 21, 1993
Government Orders
Why do I say that? I say that simply because my hon. colleague from Regina-Qu'Appelle has put forward a set of amendments which essentially delete part III of this act. He has acknowledged that to reduce government spending and wasteful government expenditures is something that he and we enthusiastically endorse and support.
When the government launches something that is regressive, that will ensure that the arts and social sciences in Canada will not proceed in the same way as they ought to, that will diminish the status of research and that will diminish the quality of education, training and research then it is something that no one in their right mind would support.
My friend from Regina-Qu'Appelle has put forward a set of amendments that say: For the sake of decency, reasonableness, the future of Canada, and jobs and opportunities for young Canadians in the future let us take this section out of this legislation.
We are not alone in this call. This bill was sent to committee so we could listen to the experts, to those who understand these issues more than ourselves, who live in this experience, and who have made a career and a profession of education and research and developing the social sciences and humanities.
Witness after witness appeared before the committee and every single one of them said to do the same thing. They said to scrap this section of the legislation because it is bad, it is wrong, and it is not in the best interest of Canada.
In a democracy part of our legislative process is to go to the people who are most knowledgeable in the area we are considering in a piece of legislation and ask them for their input. We ask for their advice and suggestions.
To be fair we do not necessarily automatically follow all of their suggestions and advice, but we accept what they have to say as being reasoned and very sensible and very important from their perspective. Based on that we make a judgment.
When there is some commonality to the extent that every single witness appearing says to do the same thing, scrap the bill, and makes long presentations as to why this would be appropriate, when not a single member of
the government can criticize what they have to say and members of the opposition support what they have to say then it becomes clear this section should be deleted.
A lot of my friends on the government benches hold that same position. I know some government members have actually lobbied the minister to get this section out of the bill. Why? I guess they are beginning to listen to their constituents for once.
There has been a great to do in the last little while about the new emerging leadership of the Conservative Party saying it is time we listened to the constituents, it is time we listened to the people of Canada. Where the hell have they been in the last eight and a half years? Is this not the way a democracy is supposed to work?
All of a sudden there is this new revelation, this great new approach, that we should try listening to the people of Canada. Now is the time for those leadership candidates to show they actually mean what they say. When we vote on this motion that would delete the section that literally all Canadians who are aware and understand this process want to see removed then we will believe what they say. Then we will believe they will actually listen to the people of Canada because they certainly have not on issues like the GST, the North American free trade agreement and others.
I listened with interest to the previous speaker from Winnipeg who said the reason that the government is doing this is to save money, to save the taxpayers' hard-earned tax dollars. If that is what this is intended to do, it does not do that. As a matter of fact, there is absolutely no saving at all.
One does not have to listen to me to make this point. We can go to the Treasury Board and see what it has to say because the Treasury Board did a very thorough analysis, as it is wont to do, of this new cultural agency. In other words, it examined amalgamating the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the international cultural program into the Canada Council.
It asked what the savings in dollars and cents by doing this would be. The Treasury Board went through all of the computer programs, the analyses and so on. Lo and behold there would be no savings in 1992, no savings in 1993-94, no savings in 1994-95, and so on and so forth. In other words, the government itself said that there is no
April 21, 1993

financial advantage to doing this. That makes a mockery out of what the government is doing.
If the point is to save taxpayers' money and the government says in its own analysis that it does not save any money, then for goodness' sake let us not use that argument.
What other argument can be used? The only other argument that can be used was reflected the other day by an individual from the other place, Conservative senator Finlay MacDonald. He was the first senator appointed by our Prime Minister and he is absolutely furious about what the government is doing. He is a Conservative member of the Upper House, the Senate, and he is furious because he says all the government is really doing is catering to the Reform Party by taking some Draconian, unnecessary, and horrible steps that will set back advanced education and research in this country for many years. The reason the government is doing that is to cater to the Reform Party and its rather outmoded and "dinosaurial" platforms.
Perhaps I should quote from the senator directly. He said: "The whole exercise is the government's attempt to feed the public perception that chronic deficits are caused by waste and mismanagement for it allows the public to believe there is a painless way to solve our serious financial problems. The whole exercise might be nothing more than a symbolic act to protect the party's right flank from attacks from the dreaded Reform Party to cause sufficient pain and spill enough blood to impress the voters. If true this might be good politics in the short term but it is not good public policy in the long run". Those are brilliant words from Senator Finlay MacDonald. He is saying what the government is doing is absolutely haywire, absolutely wrong and not in the best interest of Canada.
I want to again commend my colleague from Regina- Qu'Appelle for bringing forth this set of amendments that will now give the House of Commons an opportunity, and particularly those on the government side, to vote against including part III in this legislation and voting in favour of keeping the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the international cultural program separate in terms of funding agencies.
It is our way, as parliamentarians, to show that we acknowledge the tremendous role that social sciences
Government Orders
play these days in the future of the country. We recognize the tremendous value of the humanities in developing Canadian culture and that these should be recognized and funded separately from other funding agencies and institutions.

The fact is that in our modem society we have needs that are not properly reflected in the structure of parliamentary government. Parliamentary government in Britain was established in its present form about 150 years ago with the two-party system of government. Only a minority of men were able to vote and no women could vote. Only a minority of men and women could read and write. An urgent message from Edinburgh might be brought to London in several days by a strong rider on a relay of strong horses and it took six weeks to cross the Atlantic. I would like to explain to the House the importance of the decision being made by the government and why I personally am very opposed to it as is my caucus. I am also very supportive of the amendments being proposed by my colleague from St. Boniface.
It has taken the academic community in Canada several years to mature and develop the sophistication it now has. One of the major steps taken by the academic community was to join the government in working on the development of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.
I had the good fortune at the very early age of 31 to become a member of the board of directors just after it began in late fall, 1977. In 19781 joined it and as of April
1, 1978 I was a member of the board for the next five years. Thus I bring to the House not only my perspective as an academic and teacher for 18 years, but my views as somebody who was responsible for decision-making within the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council during its formative years.
I would like to take some time to explain to the House how we built up this organization. Those who follow the House may wonder if this is not an arcane discussion about a fairly small organization. They should consider the fact that we try to build up a series of organizations in this country one step at a time which have the capacity to research and develop good minds, reward good minds, give them the resources they need and at the same time not go around in circles.
Those who have been involved with the creative process will know that if the structures of research are not done properly, it is very difficult for people to develop careers and to have the resources to do the full research. The government at the time decided to move away from a joint organization of the Canada Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council because it found that when it came time to make decisions it was dealing with apples and oranges.
Culture is defined in terms of the theatre, music, literature, and all endeavours that are genetically under the arts. The organization of the cultural community in Canada, the organization of the arts and the organization of the creative processes of the arts are much different from the organization at work in the social sciences world which although it overlaps is different from what is done in the humanities. Most of it, although not all of it, takes place within a university setting. It requires a special type of organization to liaise not only with the individual researcher but also with the academic community.
I was impressed by the difficult task before us. For example, the university system as members know is driven mostly by provincial considerations. In the 10 provinces there are many different ways that universities are structured. Most provincial legislatures have particular acts. Therefore when spending relationships are developed with these organizations it takes a while for one organization to know another.
April 21, 1993

I can remember, for example, the question of sabbaticals was handled much differently in highly unionized situations. In the province of Quebec it was handled differently than it was in my province of Manitoba.
As a member of the board we learn from experience the significance of different methods. In the first five years of the board we managed to attract some outstanding Canadians who had previously been involved with the Canada Council. They brought to bear in the new organization not only their experiences in their host organization and/or their private lives but the work done by the Canada Council before that.

Andre was able to bring a sensitivity to the job that was appreciated by everyone. The reason I say this is that the relationship between the university world and the federal government is at best a delicate one. We are dealing with questions of ideology, the career patterns of individuals and the distance between Ottawa and some pretty remote universities. It takes a while to build up confidence within both.
We need the freedom to do the research as generated by the researcher and defined by the research community. At the same time I do not have to tell the House how important is the context of public expenditure controls, being a watch-dog organization over how government moneys are distributed.
The objectives are not easy to combine. It is not easy to ask somebody what research they are going to do, have them apply, have their work evaluated and have the money put into the community through the university or to the individual directly to make sure a product is produced and the person's career continues.

For example, for trademark matters, as part of the new intellectual property tribunal the bill contains a provision that in trademark composition no new evidence can be filed in the event that the matter is appealed to the Federal Court of Canada. Imagine that, no new evidence can be presented?
Today if you file an appeal you can file new evidence whereas in the proposed subsection no new evidence may be filed. This is a good example of the government going forward blindly, not knowing where it is headed and not doing its homework.
By removing the lines indicated, as I have proposed in the amendment, an individual would once again be allowed to submit additional evidence. This it seems to me is a most reasonable request, not unreasonable at all.
Under the system today when there is a trademark opposition evidence is filed by both sides in the form of affidavits, written arguments are filed and there is an opportunity for an oral hearing. The opposition board is chaired by a lawyer and two other hearing officers. Trademark agents then plead the cases of their clients before the board.
At the present time less than 2 per cent of these cases are appealed and hundreds of cases are heard annually. The system works well. Le systeme fonctionne bien, il ne faut pas oublier cela.
What will happen as a result of this bill? We will have a new intellectual property tribunal which hears trademark opposition cases and for which all of the evidence has to be filed before the intellectual property tribunal because no new evidence can be filed on appeal. This is not going to work. This will lead to more cross-examination and more affidavits. It will be the affidavit of the officer, the affidavits of customers in serving evidence and it will turn into a much more costly system.
The government said it wanted to save money. Here is a change that is going to cost it more money. C'est malheureux, c'est vraiment malheureux, monsieur le President, qu'ils ne comprennent pas cela.
This is why I am suggesting we remove this offensive section and once again allow additional evidence to be submitted.

There is a basic principle involved here. If the changes proposed by the government are accepted-I think regretfully it did not understand that and I hope my friend opposite will reconsider the matter-it will be impossible to submit new evidence. Everything will have to be done from the outset. The result will be extra work and therefore extra costs. Things will not go as smoothly as they do now, so why change something that is already working very well.
There is a lesson to be learned here. The government tried to make all kind of changes and came out with a massive bill which has generated a number of amendments about various organizations, and I believe the government went astray. It does not know where it is headed. It does not have a clue.
The government said in the beginning that it was introducing this bill in order to save money. Costs were supposed to go down, but that has not been proven. Then it got scared because we said: where is the proof? It argued it would improve efficiency. We said: where is the proof? Have you done any studies? It said: " No". Then we started to ask pointed questions like the one I raised a moment ago: " Did you consider this in detail?" Yes,
April 21, 1993

more or less. Obviously no thorough study of the bill was made. Elere is a reasonable proposal. If the government really wants to prove that it listens to the people, to opposition members, it has a golden opportunity to do so.

I would submit that not only this particular amendment but the other ones that I made previously are really quite reasonable. They attempt to respond to the complaints that we have heard. Many people wanted the whole thing withdrawn and the government resisted that even though it was flirting a little bit with the possibility of rescinding it.
We know that and it knows that, but the big hammer of some minister came down and said: "No way". I said: "Okay. Here are some reasonable amendments. If you were a reasonable group of people, and I think that many of you are but you probably do not have a chance to show that reasonableness, then here is an opportunity. I gave you several opportunities with the amendments that were just debated a short while ago which we have just finished debating and I am presenting another one. Surely you want to respect the basic fundamental of democracy and that is that you can submit more evidence if you want to appeal a decision, that it does not stop there".
That is it. I think I made my point, and I hope the government will support this particular amendment, as well as all the others we submitted.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak on Motion No. 65, tabled by my colleague, the hon. member for St. Boniface. I am a little disappointed by the hon. member's attitude. It is incredible to see that such a nice colleague, such a nice man is so pessimistic, has such a gloomy view of the future and doubts the efficiency of our measures. I can assure my colleague that time will show that his fears were quite groundless.
As for the savings, the opposition constantly harps on about the money we are going to save with these measures, through streamlining administrative costs.
Government Orders
They criticize us for quoting figures at random, but I will remind my colleagues that the figure of about $5 million which has been announced, as I mentioned yesterday in the House, is the result of the discussions that have taken place between the management of the Canada Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the Treasury Board. I would advise my colleagues, once and for all, to pick up the phone, it is not even a long distance call from here, and call the executive board of the Canada Council which will no doubt be happy to confirm the figures that were put forward here.
It is a commonplace for additional evidence to be tabled before the Court of Appeal and for a new lawsuit to be engaged in there. This approach is very time consuming for the judges of the Federal Court and in general it is a source of useless spending on the part of the clients. The government does not know any other instance when such a practice is tolerated in Canada.
The government feels a provision forbiding the tabling of additional evidence in the case of appeals would only eventually make the Intellectual Property Tribunal procedure consistent with all the other established practices and would allow cases to be correctly dealt with from the start. This principle follows from the analysis of the matter which can be found in the Henderson report, published in 1991, and I wish to refer my colleague to it. It is an important study on the legal controversy mechanisms, prepared by one of the most distinguished members of the Canadian legal profession. Out of that study came the recommendation for the creation of the intellectual property tribunal.
According to government data, between 15 and 30 appeals are lodged with the Federal Court each year. Therefore, contrary to what the member for St. Boniface is trying to say, the time alone spent by judges on those appeals could lead to tremendous savings.
It is a matter of common sense. One does not have to be a genius to figure it out.
Finally, the government feels that as a result of this provision forbidding the filing of new evidence a greater number of cases will be settled before the hearing. At the present time, hearings are often devoted to questioning and discovery which should be of a more informal nature.

April 21, 1993
Government Orders
The Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada seems to have concerns with the added obligation of avoiding mistakes right from the start. They feel it might jeopardize the livelihood of the trademark agents who are not lawyers. These agents are required to appear before the actual Trade Marks Opposition Board. Now the Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada fears that lawyers will be called upon to intervene more often than the agents.
The government feels this concern is unfounded. The increased efficiency of the process will probably allow the trademark agents to deal with a larger number of cases in less time and the lawyers' services will be required for the more contentious and more complex traditional legal issues.
In a competitive context, the success of our intellectual property specialists, including trademark agents, depends on efficiency.
The government has already put forward, at the committee stage, an amendment which dealt to some extent with the concern expressed by the Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada with respect to the government's decision to remove the opportunity for a new hearing of the evidence by the court under an appeal from a decision regarding a trademark invalidation or opposition procedure.
Pursuant to the amendment put forward by the government, a Federal Court judge would have the discretionary power to authorize the hearing of new evidence when circumstances warrant it, and this in order to prevent any serious injustice.
Transitional provisions are made in sections 155 and 157 of the legislation, and the hon. member for Richelieu would do better to read the bill, for he would know what he is talking about. Under those provisions, the trademark registrar continues to have jurisdiction with respect to any matter referred to him under the former regime. By registrar we also mean of course the former Trade Marks Opposition Board that has not been formally set up by a legislation.
Therefore, the adjustments to be made by the intellectual property specialists will be made gradually over a
long period of time. At the end of the day, such adjustments will serve everybody's interests, because efficiency and productivity are the objectives aimed at by all interested parties.
As for the allegations by the hon. member for St. Boniface that we should listen to people, that is precisely what we are doing. The public has clearly indicated to us that it is fed up with politicians who come here to the House claiming they have innate knowledge and propose major expenditures without any regard for the taxpayers' ability to pay, ordinary citizens, those who work 40 hours a week and try very hard to make ends meet.
We listen to these people, and they tell us that we should do what needs to be done to streamline government, to streamline our administrative costs and reduce our expenses.
I would have thought that the hon. member for Richelieu, who is so close to the people, was listening more closely to his constituents. If he went to see them more regularly and talked with them I am sure that is the message he would get from these citizens, these men and women who work 40 hours a week, who pay taxes and ask their government and their representatives to strive to cut government costs and expenses.
That is what Bill C-93 is about, no more and no less.
The hon. member for St. Boniface is wrong in saying that we do not listen to the people. Just recently we distributed 7,000 survey questionnaires in the riding of Terrebonne and received replies from 1,167 constituents who took part in a budget-making exercise. The signals we got from the riding of Terrebonne were very clear: Cut expenses and reduce the tax burden on the public.
That is what Bill C-93 does. That is why I ask the members of this House, in particular the hon. member for Richelieu who claims to be close to his people, who constantly boasts of paying attention to his constituency, to do the honourable thing once and for all in this House for their constituents; respect their ability to pay. He should stop being partisan and engaging in petty, partisan politics and quit his empty rhetoric. He should do something positive in this House and support a bill to reduce government spending and the tax burden on the taxpayers in his riding and mine, in Quebec and across Canada.
April 21, 1993

I think that would be the most honourable thing the hon. member for St. Boniface and all opposition members should do, out of respect for all Canadians' ability to pay.
Therefore I urge hon. members to reject Motion No. 65 because it is not realistic. It is not in keeping with the intent of the bill, the purpose of which is to increase efficiency and reduce costs.

Mr. Speaker, it certainly amazes me when I listen to government members justifying their actions.
They start out by saying that these measures are undertaken to reduce costs and the deficit. With regard to that nobody has any problem. We want to see costs, deficits and debt reduced absolutely. We have no problem with that whatsoever.
However we maintain that what the government is doing is actually increasing the debt and the deficit. We have heard previous debates dealing with part III of Bill C-93. We have introduced evidence from documents obtained under access to information in which the Department of Finance shows that there are no net savings to the measures this government is taking by abolishing SSHRC and the cultural programs of external Affairs and rolling them all into the Canada Council.
We have demonstrated that there are no savings. In fact, we can assume it is going to cost money. What we are hearing now is that there is a need to move into a new building. There is the cost of integrating these three different functions. This costs more money than was originally anticipated. This is costing money.
We are dealing with an amendment which is worthy. The government is trying to defend its opposition to this amendment introduced by my colleague from the Liberal Party on the basis of cost.
I was just reading the submission in committee by Mr. Robert D. Gould who is a member of the Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada. He has a fair amount to say about this section. What this section does is to
Government Orders
prevent new evidence from being introduced on an appeal to the Trade Marks Opposition Board. This gentleman says:
Under the system today, when there is a trademark opposition, evidence is filed by both sides in the form of affidavits, written arguments are filed, and there is an opportunity for an oral hearing. The Trade Marks Opposition Board is chaired by a lawyer, having close to two decades of experience in these trademark matters on the board, ably assisted by two other hearing officers. Trademark agents who are lawyers or who are not lawyers plead the cases of their clients before the board. There can be cross-examination of affidavit evidence, although this takes place in less than 5 per cent of the cases, and the entire procedure is summary in nature and not extremely expensive.
Less than 2 per cent of all cases decided by this Trade Marks Opposition Board are appealed and hundreds of cases are heard annually, so the system works well. For those cases that are appealed the parties are able to file additional evidence on appeal and, I repeat, that is only in 2 per cent of the cases.
Now, what is going to happen when, as a result of this budgetary process, we have a new intellectual property tribunal, which hears trademark opposition cases and for which all the evidence, for now and for all time, has to be filed before the Intellectual Property Tribunal because no new evidence can be filed on appeal.
Do you think there is going to be cross-examination in only 5 per cent of the cases? Hardly. Because this is a person's last chance, I would expect there will be cross-examinations going on in the majority of cases. Then, what about a small Canadian company that is the applicant or the opponent and that is going to file today perhaps the affidavit of its officer?
Under the new system, where this is your last chance, it will be the affidavit of the officer, the affidavit of customers, and survey evidence, and it is going to turn into a much more costly exercise.
I estimate to clients I deal with that the cost of an evidence stage of an opposition is between approximately $1,000 and $2,000.
Then in his testimony he is suggesting that under the new system it is going to cost $10,000 to $20,000. He suggested as well in his testimony that now lawyers are going to become involved in the process.
Here is his summation:
I would submit that it is not an answer to say that this provision about no new evidence is going to be deferred.
We heard the government members saying that they will not implement this right away.
If it is not worthy of being in the legislation today, or implemented today, surely if it does become worthy at some time in the future, that is the time to put it in.

April 21, 1993
Government Orders
Basically what he is saying is that this provision under the act that will not allow new evidence to be introduced on appeal is going to cost more money. It is going to cost more money for those people who have failed themselves on this process and it is going to cost the government more money.
Here we see again in this particular provision that the government is going to end up having a greater debt as we see with the previous part III of this bill that abolishes SSHRC and that is going to cost the government more money.
A few weeks ago there was a study that looked at the cuts to the Canada Council. It came to the conclusion that the government was going to lose more money with the cuts to the Canada Council than it was going to gain because of those cuts. This study showed that because of these cuts there were going to be fewer taxes collected and fewer cultural industries producing things and employing people. There was going to be an increase in welfare, an increase in unemployment insurance and the net effect was going to be a decrease in government revenues.
We see how this government's attempt to reduce its costs and to reduce the deficit that it has the opposite results. It is no wonder that after more than eight years of the Tory government's attempt to reduce the debt and deficit we have seen the deficit double because these people across the way do not know how to use their intelligence to start reducing government waste and government costs. Every time it turns around and introduces a measure it only increases the debt of the country.
It is no wonder that after eight years of Tory attempts to control expenditures we have seen our deficit double. It is because of measures found in Bill C-93 that we begin to understand why our deficit and why our debt has doubled over the last eight years. This government in its pigheadedness insists on introducing measures that in the end will cost Canadian taxpayers more money.
It is about time we had a new government.

keep up their good work. However, when the time comes to define our sovereignty we will take our share of that tribunal, as long as it is still in the interests of our people and has not been dismantled, which is exactly what the government wants to do with this bill. Mr. Speaker, I would just like to know if my colleague, the parliamentary secretary, recognizes that the government made a mistake. He only has to nod, because I think several mistakes were made, although the last one we saw was a bit different. Is that so? Am I right?

Mr. Speaker, the fact that I was nodding does not mean that I endorse in any way the remarks made by the hon. member. I would like to make it clear though that we on the government side recognize that we are not perfect. Perfection is something we leave to the opposition.
Sometimes we need to make some adjustments. The legislative process that we have in Canada, with all its different stages, including second reading stage, legislative committee stage, report stage and third reading stage, is designed to allow us to make technical or other adjustments when necessary, for the benefit of the Canadian people.
Therefore it cannot be said that this amendment results from an error but rather from the desire of the Canadian government to do things right, as is always the case.

Mr. Speaker, I rise somewhat amused. First of all I wish to go on record as also supporting the amendment. It is a technical amendment. It is one in which the government corrects what was imperfectly drafted to begin with.
April 21, 1993

I fully sympathize with the parliamentary secretary's explanation. Of course as human beings, and this being a human institution, we are quite capable of making mistakes. The ability of correcting those mistakes has to be natural.
That is why legislation goes through the various stages. Each stage should be like a filter. We give critical examination of the legislation. As things come out in debate, in consideration and critical analysis those things that are seen not to be quite right are corrected.
I just wish the government would take that principle and extend it a little further. During the debate if the government was really honest, not in a partisan mood, not in a mood of saying this is what we have brought down and this is what we are going to force through, but rather if the government was more open, it would realize the things that had been brought forward in the debate on this bill, whether at second reading, in committee or report stage, that where it hoped there would be savings there was not going to be savings.
Some of the things that are still in Bill C-93 are going to create more hardship and more cost rather than making things efficient and reducing cost. We have pointed this out. Members of the academic community have pointed things out. People involved in patent and patent rights have pointed these things out.
Unfortunately, the government has not been listening. It might have been listening but it is not hearing. This is of course we find unfortunate. If our parliamentary system worked properly and we were able to set aside our partisan differences, then on a matter like Bill C-93 we should have been able to have many more significant changes that would have been good for this country, would have been good for the people, those parts of Bill C-93 which are supposed to serve.
Again, we will support the government amendment. Our only wish is that the principle would be extended as well to other sections and other recommendations and amendments that we have introduced.

Motion No. 67
That Bill C-93 be amended in clause 17 of schedule I by striking out line 40 at page 82 and substituting the following therefor:
"regulations imposing, on any licensing body, licensee or user".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have an opinion that I would like to put on the record. This would give the government another opportunity to make a correction and respond to the series of very reasonable amendments. I am hoping that my colleague from Terrebonne, among others, will get an opportunity to examine it carefully and perhaps support it.
I want to read that opinion into the record to make sure it is not misunderstood. It reads as follows:
That the word "assignee" is not an appropriate use of the term in the amendment because SOCAN is in fact an assignee of copyrights. Also, copyright holders should be removed from the amendment because it will spread the liability for costs to all of SOCAN's members since they are the legal copyright holders.
Those are important points that need to be recognized. Here is an opinion of someone who believes this current legislation is improperly worded:
The problem with Bill C-93, section 17(2) as it now stands is that SOCAN, a clearing house that collects fees for the users of creators' works and distributes these fees to the creators is liable for a large portion of the costs associated with the operation of the intellectual property tribunal.

April 21, 1993
