These costs as indicated by the officials at yesterday's hearings
could amount to well over $1 million annually.
That is a direct quote of an opinion that was sent to me and the government as well, I believe, so it could examine the current bill. There is one more paragraph:
This is fundamentally unfair since other parties, namely the users
of creative works, also benefit from the operation of the tribunal.
These parties should also be responsible for the tribunal's costs.
Again, I want to make a plea to the government to look at this. It does not seem to be unreasonable. It seems to have made an excellent point. I hope it will be examined carefully. It would be unfortunate to pass this bill and have to change it later.
Let me summarize the conclusions of the analysis that were done for me on this bill. I would like to enter them into the record.
SOCAN opposes the introduction of those provisions of Bill C-93 that provide the proposed intellectual property tribunal with the power to fix both the costs of particular proceedings and the costs of the tribunal generally.
The process of the approval of royalties for the performance of musical works is not apt for the imposition of these cost provisions. Alternatively, if it is decided that the principle of user pay tribunal must become a feature of the proposed intellectual property tribunal, the statute should be amended to set out guidelines in the statute and not regulations. They should clearly provide guidance to the tribunal and ensure that licensing bodies are consulted in determining the nature and extent of those costs and the manner in which the licensing bodies can pass those costs on to their licen-cees.
Licensing bodies should also be given the right to appeal any decision that may determine those costs for which they will be responsible. To treat these costs as proposed in Bill C-93 amounts to a tax on the incomes of composers, lyricists and songwriters. It is grossly unfair to them.
There are a few points that need to be underlined. [Translation]
It seems to me that this opinion, which I think is shared by the government, clearly indicates some weaknesses in this bill. In its present form, the bill is too vague, and that could cause some very serious difficulties. There are principles of fundamental injustice in this bill. I would simply ask the government to consider what was said, what I just proposed, so that I and the people I represent can be sure the whole bill will reflect the remarks I just made.
As I said earlier, it would be unfortunate to proceed with this enormous bill only to find in it the kind of potential errors I just pointed out.
I am sure you will recall, Mr. Speaker, because you have an excellent memory, that I suggested a few minutes ago, when we studied Motion No. 65, that there may be some serious errors in that part of the bill also. The government brought forward this enormous bill, so enormous that it got lost in it. I am beginning to fear that, because I am an opposition member, the government will not listen to what I said. In fact, the suggestion did not come from me, but from someone else, and I thought it made sense. That is why I make those recommendations to the government.
[English)
There are some potential traps in this particular bill. I outlined some in Motion No. 65 and in Motion No. 67 with my amendments. I would like the government to simply look at them. I hope they will not be simply discarded because I am a member of the opposition. Remember that these are professional opinions that have been entered into the record from responsible people who are really quite concerned.
If the government proceeds with the bill without looking at this I believe it would be irresponsible on my part not to call it irresponsible. I hope the comments I have entered into the record and shared in openness and sincerity will be looked at and I will be given some reason why they are not acceptable if that is the case.
Perhaps I am dreaming but I would like to hear some good reasons why this whole series of amendments I proposed would not be respected. They seem to be minimal changes that respond to the needs and expressed concerns of Canadians who have a lot of information about this bill.
April 21, 1993

I believe I have made my point. I look forward to a rebuttal of the points I have entered into the record. Failing that rebuttal, I will assume that the government supports my amendments.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Marc Robitaille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
To start with, Mr. Speaker, I would say that it is perfectly normal for people to express concern. However, for a member of this House there are always two alternatives: members either fuel that concern or they try to calm things down. That is what I was trying to do for the benefit of the hon. member for St. Boniface.
If this proposal was agreed to, the government would have to widen the scope of the cost recovery provisions in order to be able to charge directly to users, licensees and consumers the costs associated with creative works administered by a licensing body.
SOCAN, the only body as such to stand against the government proposal to charge user fees to clients of the intellectual property tribunal, is indeed requesting that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Boniface be adopted. This amendment would widen the scope of cost recovery provisions and allow for charging directly to users, licensees and consumers the costs associated with creative work administered by the licensing body. The government's policy is to recover the costs from the licensing body which could then bill users according to economic conditions approved by the intellectual property tribunal.
Thanks to the application of user fees with the option of cost recovery in the sector under the board's jurisdiction, the copyright system will operate like many other government services which recover real operating costs from users instead of making all taxpayers bear these costs.
The National Energy Board and the CRTC are two good examples of this practice. Both agencies have the discretionary power to recover costs from users as appropriate, and they do so from time to time. However, the agencies are under no obligation to do so. The United States has a similar system with its copyright royalty tribunal. Here again, there are no specific rules
Government Orders
providing for cost recovery from users, licencees or consumers.
I would like to make it clear to hon. members, and more particularly to the hon. member for St. Boniface, that the government's proposal will represent savings of over $1.2 million annually for taxpayers. SOCAN revenues, which are all under the jurisdiction of the proposed intellectual property tribunal, represent about $70 million of the $120 million now covered by the Copyright Board. As new licensing bodies are created, for instance in the photocopy sector, the share of costs billed to SOCAN will diminish.
The purpose of the new provisions of part VII of Bill C-93 is to guarantee that the principal clients of the intellectual property tribunal, including SOCAN, the Canadian Motion Picture Distributors Association and photocopy licensing bodies, will assume a fair share of the tribunal's operating costs. A cost recovery system based on user fees will not come into effect until the appropriate regulations have been drafted and put in place. Details of the system cannot be worked out until the regulatory process has begun. This process will include broad consultation with interested parties and consultation and co-operation between those parties and the government.
It is very difficult to recover costs directly from licencees and consumers who, ultimately, pay the royalties passed on to creators by the licensing bodies. SOCAN alone has more than 35,000 licencees, ranging from major cable network companies and the CBC, down to restaurants and church basement auditoriums.
In Motion No. 67, the term user may be interpreted as including consumers, who total 25 million in Canada. It is preferable to give the proposed intellectual property tribunal the discretionary power to recover costs instead of providing for a system by regulations or legislation. Furthermore, it would be very difficult and extremely complex to develop detailed provisions that would cover the broad range of users, licencees and consumers.
Finally we would like to point out that the only licensing body opposed to the cost recovery principle proposed in this bill is SOCAN. Consequently, the government cannot accept any amendments at this stage. The legitimate concerns of SOCAN can be dealt with most effectively during the regulatory process and

April 21, 1993
Government Orders
through the submission of briefs to the intellectual property tribunal.
The motion is unacceptable because it would lead to a policy that would be neither sound nor practical. It is practically impossible to develop a specific system for billing costs to the many and various classes of users, licencees and consumers for works that are administered collectively for licensing purposes. Licensing bodies will probably obtain the desired results through the far more effective approach of billing costs where appropriate.
Consequently I would urge all members to reject this amendment, for the reasons just mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, I really tried to follow what the parliamentary secretary was saying but I am afraid I am going to have to wait until I read Hansard tomorrow. I think what the parliamentary secretary was doing was just reading out what bureaucrats had told him to read out.
It is a technical amendment. There are technicalities in it. I am not quite certain the parliamentary secretary totally understood what he was saying but I suspect what was happening is that he was given something to read by some bureaucrats. It sure sounded bureaucratic to me.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to give the Chair and the hon. member who alluded to the fact that I was reading a text the assurance that this is not-

speechtext: I cannot allow this point of order because if I did we would have constant interruptions. In this House members may differ in their opinions of the behaviour or statements of their colleagues, but they cannot seek a remedy from the Chair.

Mr. Speaker, I was not objecting at all to the hon. member referring to his notes quite often. I was wishing that he would have expressed the concepts and the government's arguments in his own words. Had he
done so I think we would have all understood the arguments a little bit better.
The problem is that when bureaucrats write these briefing notes the bureaucrats have their own language. It is a language that I find at times hard to understand. Particularly when the bureaucrats are trained in law they have sentences that run through half the page and quite often are hard to understand. It takes another bureaucrat to totally understand the argument they are making.
SOCAN made a representation to our committee and I thought at the time that it made some sense. I did not think that government members or people from the government departments succeeded in refuting their concerns.
What is the situation? SOCAN represents the composers, lyricists and so forth, the creators of musical works. It collects certain royalties and fees. To establish the level of royalties and fees it goes to the board that is being created here. It has to do this. It is not a choice on its part. It has to go through this process. There is no problem with that and SOCAN does not have any problem with that.
The users of their musical works also have the right to make presentations to the board if they object to this provision or that fee and so forth. I do not think anybody has any problem with that. That is due process. SOCAN goes and presents its fees and then the users who have to pay those fees have the opportunity to give their objections and comments. SOCAN objects to the fact that the cost is entirely borne by them.
The parliamentary secretary is wrong when he states that SOCAN is against the principle of cost recovery and user fees. From reading and remembering its testimony before our committee I can say that was not the argument it was making. The argument it was making is that the cost should be borne by all the parties concerned.
Let us say I am a restaurateur, as I was before becoming a member of this august body, and let us say I have a sound system that works and that I should pay a fee to SOCAN. I do not like the fee but I am an ornery son of a gun and I am going to go on the war-path and create as much trouble as I can for SOCAN so I appeal and do all kinds of harassments. I do not have to pay any of the cost. SOCAN has to pay all the cost. Therefore
April 21, 1993

SOCAN is exposed to all sorts of nuisance actions against it. The people initiating that action bear no costs but SOCAN has to carry all the cost. From what I understand that is SOCAN's argument, and I think it is a reasonable argument.
I wish the government would get off its high horse and listen to these arguments and begin to recognize that perhaps this should be changed a little. It does not require a major change, it does not require a change from the basic principle of cost recovery. All we are asking for is some change to make certain that if a group brings nuisance actions it too will carry the cost and not just SOCAN itself, not just the composers and lyricists, the people who create the musical works. They should not be the only ones that carry the cost of this.
It seems fair to me. It seems just to me. What is the government's problem on this? Why can it not see this? Why is it not more conciliatory, more willing to work with all the actors, with the opposition, with the users of the services in making certain that we have good legislation that everybody can live with? Why will the government not be a little more constructive?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words on this very important amendment. Once again, it is an amendment from the opposition which would be very easy for the government to accept, since it would not translate into costs to the government and it would merely ensure the sharing of the costs of an appeal before a tribunal for users as well, in addition to collectives or copyright associations.
A nation grows and lives through its creative talents. If a nation such as the Canadian or Quebec nation exists, it is because it has had artists and creative minds in the scientific field and in every other field, especially at the artistic level. This is often what identifies a nation, and it is said that a great nation emerges when its composers and creative minds are at the top of their profession through their publications and the way they are accepted by the public.
France exists and rose through its great authors, the same way the Americans spread their culture through
Government Orders
their musical composers and their creative talents, especially in the field of movies.
However, in Quebec and in Canada we are a third world country. In terms of the way copyrights are treated, as well as the status of the artist, we are several years behind, even though the government opposite made a little step forward with Bill C-88, as I recall following pressures from various organizations.
However in this case, as in Bill C-62, we are dealing with copyrights. I talked to the president of the association des auteurs-compositeurs du Quebec, who told me how unusual the situation was. For example, the owner of a public place-we talked earlier about restaurants, but we could also have mentioned public waiting rooms or shopping centres-can decide to challenge, before the tribunal, the fact that he has to pay copyrights for musical works which he uses to attract clients and to provide them with the most comfortable environment. Therefore he pays for a picture on the wall. He pays for a chair, but he refuses to pay when he fulfils the dream of those people waiting in the emergency room, in the restaurant or in the bar. Then there is a challenge.
He finds himself before a court, oftentimes on an appeal, and sometimes he loses, but the costs will be billed to the management corporation. In that sense, the amendment is very important since it proposes to add the user to the list and, in doing so, it could put an end to some abuses. Government says it wants to ensure better management, to cut down on expenditures. However if it wants these agencies to spend less it should not open the door to anyone who wishes to challenge anything for any reason whatsoever, however bizarre. Instead it should say: Very well, you want to challenge so you will have to share the costs if you lose your case just like you would in any other court.
This is what this amendment is all about. It would not cost the government a cent. This amendment is a salute to our artists who make it possible for our two nations to come together, a salute to those artists, especially those from Quebec to whom I want to pay tribute, who created that new nation which will soon become sovereign and will join the group of world nations.

April 21, 1993
Government Orders
It is the same for the Canadian nation; Canadian creators also played a part in the shaping of Canada and when our two nations will engage in a neighbourly-
You will always be welcome among us.

My colleague, the member for St. Boniface, tells me we will always be welcome. You will too. Besides, it is obvious that in our thinking about sovereignty we will no doubt suggest that all those who wish to, either Canadian or Quebecer, will be able to get both a Canadian and a Quebec passport. We will also propose an agreement, some form of trade relations as there should be between civilized countries. In any case, trade relations exist automatically among countries bound by great international agreements.
As far as respect for both nations is concerned, I am quite convinced that the Quebec nation and the Canadian nation will maintain a very respectful relationship and will co-operate toward their mutual success.
In that respect, as I was saying a minute ago, before my friend from St-Boniface's interjection, these amendments will allow our authors to have a better income, not necessarily in terms of salary but in terms of decreased costs for collecting royalties from public places for instance. These amendments will allow the Societe des auteurs-compositeurs du Quebec, or SOCAN, the society which manages Canadian authors and composers, to act more freely to collect as well as to redistribute dues more rapidly without constantly facing complaints from people who have no right to do so since they are using the music, words, material and brainpower of authors.
In that respect, I think the tribunal should also be allowed to decide whether or not to consult users when setting ways to calculate and pay costs.
I will end on that point. I wish that Quebec members, those who are constantly forgetting that they should be promoting Quebec's interests within the government, those who choose to stay within the government, those who represent 40 per cent of the government caucus, would wake up. They should pay attention to what authors are asking of them. They should stop being yes men and become passionate promoters of Quebec interests.
They still have a golden opportunity to do so.
I want to remind them that this bill on which we will have a vote later is completely rejected by the minister, not a sovereignist minister, but by the minister Cannon from Quebec, who says: "No, this bill must be amended". He has made incredible claims about telecommunications. Even his predecessor, Mrs. Hebert, used to say when she talked about the control the federal government still had on the telecommunications bill: "It would be worse than the Meech Lake failure if this bill was passed."
We realize again to which extent, whether it be the unemployment insurance bill or the electoral reform bill, our hon. members from Quebec have an important part to play within the government. Instead of following the set course of action they must try to direct it with the help of their colleagues. We have reached the point of saying that when a Conservative member winks in Ottawa he opens an eye. It shows how passive the Conservative members are in the House. Instead of defending the government, they should defend the interests of their constituencies and of Quebec.
Aagain they miss the boat and they remind me sometimes of my mother-in-law. They stand at the edge of a financial abyss, after the constitutional failure and the economical failure, they wrap themselves in the Canadian flag and say: "I am going to jump and the flag will open like a parachute to bring me to the promised land." This reminds me of my mother-in-law. She dreams that Celine Dion is getting married and the pope is coming to sing at her wedding. Dreams are not for real. I too dream that Chretien and Mulroney become gas station attendants. However this will not come true. So the hon. members who are dreaming must wake up.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak on Bill C-102, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, the Excise Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Customs Act, the Criminal Code and a related act, as reported with amendments from the legislative committee.
Although the name of the bill relates to tax and taxation it has other implications including health. As I understand the bill, there are four measures being presented in it.
One, there will be tighter controls on the distribution and sale of duty-free tobacco products. Two, there will be improved markings on tobacco products to better identify duty-free tobacco products. Third, there will be the addition of proceeds of crime provisions to the Excise Act and Customs Act to enable law enforcement agencies to seize the proceeds of crime. This could be a big deterrent. Finally, there will be the imposition of higher penalties for smugglers and sellers of contraband goods.
That is the intent of this bill. In essence, by allowing this to proceed it could impose an increase in export taxes and impose higher fines on smugglers and sellers of contraband. As well, it will also help stop tax evasion.
I should say at the outset that the root cause of smuggling in this country is moral decadence and the absence of a public sense of duty to fellow citizens. When that duty to fellow citizens to protect their health is omitted then there is really a danger to our nation.
I submit that when we allow the sacrifice of human lives and greed for money to run a personal business of smuggling then there is really something wrong with our

April 21, 1993

country. We ought to undertake as a nation any means we can marshal to stop this moral cancer.
The implications in this bill go beyond taxation itself. They go to the area of health care. There are also implications in this bill for the tobacco farmers and there are implications for workers in the tobacco industry.
I would like the government to have a multi-faceted approach, not a patchwork or piecemeal approach, to increasing taxation thereby decreasing smuggling and the consumption of cigarettes. These are all excellent goals that we hope to attain as a country.
In so doing there is no doubt that there will be hardships and difficulties on the tobacco farmers and there will be hardships and difficulties on the workers in the tobacco industry. We must have alternative programs for those workers. We must have government aid.

Mr. Speaker, certainly the point made was that we would like members of the government side to listen to the debate.
The debate about the health of our nation and the health of our citizens is so important that we ought to have a minister of the government present in the House of Commons. It is a point well taken by one of my colleagues.

We must have programs to help the farmers diversify their crops during the transition period as the sale of tobacco decreases.
We must have training programs for the workers so they can acquire the skills to face the new challenges in fields other than the tobacco industry.
I would like to state very clearly as the critic for the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party of Canada, that we support increased taxation on cigarettes as part of the over-all strategy to decrease the consumption of tobacco and cigarettes in this country.
This is only part of the over-all strategy. Taxes alone are not enough. We say categorically it is the official Liberal policy that we will not roll back taxes on cigarettes.
What do I say about those who control the policies in the tobacco industry? We have to challenge them and their consciences so they do not direct life-style advertising at our young Canadians.
It is known that if we are able to prevent people from smoking before the age of 18 years they are much less likely to smoke later on. What a tremendous success. I should say to our tobacco industry that is concerned about the success of our anti-smoking policy that we can be a model for other countries.
April 21, 1993

It is difficult. It is a dilemma because we would like to support the workers in this industry and the source of the product, the farmers, as well. However we have to help them with other programs because the industry producing cigarettes is about the only industry that truly produces a product that harms Canadians. It leads to harm.
The harm to the Canadian citizen starts even before birth. It affects the growing child, adolescents and adults. We know the human toll in terms of disability from disease caused by smoking. It affects the lungs. It causes the destruction of our air sacs. It causes obstruction of air flow. The afflicted citizen has difficulty breathing, yet continues to live for a long time with the disability. It exacts a human toll on the quality of life of that Canadian citizen afflicted with the smoking habit. It also impacts on the productivity of that citizen in the labour force.
It also leads to other diseases. It is a significant cause of heart disease and cancer, particularly of the lungs. When you put this all together it shortens the life span.
After a period of time smoking becomes an addiction that is not easily broken. The government must have programs to help those addicted to stop the habit of smoking.
Cigarette smoking has also led to fires and the loss of homes. The toll it exacts on the human person in terms of disability and illness impacts on our medicare system in the course of delivering health care. The cost of our medicare system would go down considerably if we could prevent a number of illnesses related to smoking.
As we look at Bill C-102 let us not forget that we must also challenge the manufacturers of cigarettes to stop directing their life-style advertising at youth so they do not start smoking.
We should also have programs to help those who are already smoking but not yet addicted stop their habit while it is still sheer habit and not an addiction.
Let us also provide counselling services for those afflicted. Let us have a government program to help distribute the nicotine patch and instruct people in its
Government Orders
proper use. We congratulated the government when the change in labelling was passed recently. It is an issue that this critic from the Liberal caucus has demanded from this government since 1989 when I was first elected to this House.
We welcome increased fines to vendors to prevent them from selling cigarettes to our youth.
We should also delete the industries' names when they sponsor sporting and cultural events.
In this position taken strongly by the Liberal Party we have the support not only of those opposed to smoking for the reasons I have indicated, but the support of the smokers who would like to break the habit.
The Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Heart and Stroke Foundation and many other health groups support us and many Canadians in our efforts to have an over-all strategy to help stop smoking.
In conclusion, Bill C-102 is truly a challenge to leadership. When things are good in the country and there are no problems there is almost no need for strong leadership because there is agreement. When hard choices have to be made there is a real call to leadership.
We want to send the message that the smuggling must stop. It is inherently morally decadent and the continued practice of smuggling and selling contraband affects many Canadians.
We also want to indicate that we care about the tobacco farmers and the workers in the industry. When we have the opportunity to form the government after the next election we will have programs for them so we can truly have a consensus in this country.
I challenge this government to seek international co-operation. It must talk to the United States government and President Clinton and tell them to follow our example. In that case there will be almost no opportunity for smugglers to make a packet on the health of Canadian citizens. We need a comprehensive approach.
I am delighted to have spoken on this bill. The Official Opposition supports this bill because we feel it will help stop smuggling to a great degree.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too, along with my colleague from Thunder Bay, had the privilege to serve on the Standing Committee on Transport. It saw members from the government side and Her Majesty's Official Opposition, as well as the third party, work together to conclude a process that will see the modernization of Canada's existing legislation concerning the carriage of goods by water by adopting on a gradual basis the two international conventions known as the Hague-Visby rules and the Hamburg rules. Until that committee meeting I did not know what the Hamburg rules were. It turned out that they were a lot more than two all-beef patties, special sauce, lettuce and cheese.
In the absence of an industry-wide agreement on the adoption of either of the two rules the stage approach represents a compromise that ensures that the Canadian law is at least in step, and this is what we had a concern with in committee, with that of our trading partners.
We too will co-operate with the government on the passage of Bill C-83.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a couple of brief comments.
We are obviously supporting the legislation as we did in committee and as we did at second reading. However, I think the public does not appreciate the kind of work that members of Parliament do and that there are a lot of pieces of legislation that are processed through this House that are not partisan in any way. They are reviewed in a thoughtful and conscientious manner by members of all sides of the House. They come from the departments. In this case it was the Department of Transport but it could be Employment and Immigration, Revenue or what have you. We look at them and seem them as appropriate mechanism and appropriate changes to bring the laws into today's time.
These two bills, the one before us and the previous one, are examples of that. We looked at them. We talked to people who had concerns about them. In some cases we made some minor modifications but basically they were good pieces of legislative work.
Too often in the press we are seen as combatants as opposed to partners in making Canada work. These two bills are examples of the kind of work we do here on a regular basis.

Mr. Speaker, I concur with my friend from Thunder Bay. He is absolutely right. In short order government members, members of the Official Opposition and members of the NDP worked together on these two bills. It was not an easy piece of work: we had to sit down and had to read over these things.
Obviously we trust each other to a certain extent but there always has to be that check and balance when it comes to legislation before the House. Therefore we spent some time sitting in our offices between the hours
